prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "COMCAST CORP" (ticker CMCSA), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "CMCSA", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Comcast Corporation
markets: Mobile wireless (Xfinity Mobile, MVNO on Verizon)
TV networks and streaming (NBC, Telemundo, Peacock, Sky)
Film and TV studios (Universal, DreamWorks, Illumination)
UK and European pay-TV and broadband (Sky)

mission.plain: Comcast wants to connect people to the internet and to the shows, movies, sports and parks they love.

about.plain: Comcast runs Xfinity, which brings internet, cable TV and phone service into tens of millions of American homes and businesses through its wires. It also owns NBCUniversal, which makes TV shows and movies, runs NBC and the Peacock streaming app, and owns the Universal Studios theme parks. In Europe it owns Sky, a big TV and internet company. In 2026 it spun off most of its cable TV channels as Versant and plans to split NBCUniversal and Sky into a separate company.
about.customers: Households and businesses that pay monthly for internet, TV and phone, advertisers, TV distributors, moviegoers and theme park visitors.
about.everyday: If your home internet or cable box says Xfinity, you watch the Olympics or Sunday Night Football on NBC or Peacock, or you have ridden a ride at Universal Studios, you have used Comcast.

money.plain: ads and fees from NBC, cable channels, Peacock and Sky channels
monthly Xfinity and Sky TV subscriptions
monthly Xfinity broadband service in US homes
Universal films, DreamWorks and TV shows sold to theaters and streamers
Universal parks tickets, hotels and merchandise, including Epic Universe opened in 2025
Xfinity Mobile phone plans sold to its internet customers

result.summary: Comcast has real but eroding advantages: it owns wired networks passing more than 65 million US homes and businesses, high-value content and parks (Universal, NBC, Peacock), and scale in programming and advertising. But its core broadband franchise is losing customers to fiber and fixed-wireless rivals (domestic broadband fell from 32.3 million in mid-2023 to 31.3 million at end-2025 and lost 144,000 more in Q3 2026), and pay TV is in secular decline, so its moat is narrowing rather than widening.

pricingPower.evidence: Comcast historically raised broadband prices yearly and grew domestic broadband revenue to $25,837M in 2025 from $24,999M in 2023 while customers fell, but competition from fiber and 5G home internet forced a 2025-26 pivot to simpler, guaranteed-price plans and free wireless lines, broadband customers kept falling (net loss of 144,000 in Q3 2026) and Connectivity & Platforms revenue fell 2.7% in Q3 2026.

moats.evidence: NBCUniversal owns valuable IP (Universal Pictures, Illumination's Minions, DreamWorks, Jurassic World) and the NBC, Telemundo and Sky brands, but the Xfinity brand carries a reputation for poor service rather than loyalty.

Bundling broadband, mobile (9.3 million wireless lines at end-2025) and TV raises the hassle of leaving, but customers can and do switch to fiber or 5G home internet with little cost, as shown by broadband customer losses every recent quarter.
Broadband, pay TV and parks gain little from more users; only advertising scale and Peacock's sports audience show mild network-type benefits.

Comcast is one of the largest US media and connectivity companies ($123.7 billion revenue in 2025), giving it buying power for programming, sports rights (NBA from 2025, NFL, Olympics) and network equipment, though Charter became the larger US cable operator after closing its Cox deal in August 2026.

In most of its footprint the economics support only one cable network, so Comcast faces at most one or two wired rivals, but fiber overbuilds by AT&T and Verizon and fixed-wireless from T-Mobile and Verizon have broken that local duopoly.
Comcast is the incumbent being counter-positioned against by cord-cutting streamers and fixed-wireless carriers, not the disruptor.
It is a capable operator of networks and parks (Epic Universe opened in May 2025) but nothing in its processes is clearly impossible for rivals to copy.

Its physical cable plant and rights-of-way, long-term NFL Sunday Night Football and Olympics media rights, Universal's film library and park land in Orlando are scarce assets competitors cannot easily replicate.

customers.evidence: Comcast/Xfinity has long scored below average in customer satisfaction; in ACSI's 2026 study the ISP industry averaged 73 and Xfinity Fiber scored 77, but the company keeps losing broadband customers (31,842k at end-2024 to 31,255k at end-2025) and 274,000 video customers in Q3 2026 alone, while management says customer satisfaction is only now improving.

talent.evidence: Comcast NBCUniversal ranked No. 10 on the Fortune/Great Place to Work 100 Best Companies to Work For in 2024 (seventh consecutive year on the list), and it attracts media and tech talent, though large layoffs and restructuring around the Versant spin-off and planned NBCUniversal split weigh on morale.

product.evidence: Xfinity offers multi-gig speeds over a hybrid fiber-coax network and the Xfinity Fiber product scored 77 in ACSI 2026, above the 73 ISP average, while Peacock (48 million paid subscribers in Q3 2026) and Universal parks are strong, but fiber rivals (AT&T Fiber 79) are rated better and its TV product is in decline.

competitors.name: Charter Communications (Spectrum)
competitors.note: Largest US cable operator after buying Cox in August 2026; competes in broadband, mobile, video and business services, mostly in adjacent rather than the same towns.

competitors.name: AT&T
competitors.note: Fiber broadband overbuilding Comcast's footprint, plus wireless; AT&T Fiber leads ACSI satisfaction scores.

competitors.name: Verizon Communications
competitors.note: Fios fiber and 5G Home Internet compete for broadband; Verizon's network also hosts Xfinity Mobile.

competitors.name: T-Mobile US
competitors.note: Fastest-growing 5G fixed-wireless home internet provider and rival for mobile lines and bundles.

competitors.name: Optimum Communications (formerly Altice USA)
competitors.note: Cable broadband and TV operator in the New York area and other markets; competes for pay TV and broadband customers and programming.

competitors.name: Netflix
competitors.note: Leading streaming service competing with Peacock and pay TV for viewers' time and with NBCUniversal for content and talent.

competitors.name: Walt Disney
competitors.note: Head-to-head rival in theme parks (Walt Disney World vs Universal Orlando), studios, ABC/ESPN networks and Disney+/Hulu streaming.

competitors.name: Alphabet (YouTube, YouTube TV)
competitors.note: YouTube is the most-watched TV streaming platform in the US, and YouTube TV is a large virtual pay-TV rival; also competes for ad dollars.

competitors.name: Warner Bros. Discovery
competitors.note: Studios, HBO Max and cable networks compete with NBCUniversal; agreed in 2026 to be acquired by Paramount Skydance.

competitors.name: Paramount Skydance
competitors.note: CBS, Paramount+ and Paramount Pictures compete with NBC, Peacock and Universal for viewers, sports rights and advertisers.

competitors.name: SpaceX (Starlink)
competitors.note: Satellite broadband alternative, mainly in rural areas outside most of Comcast's footprint.

marketShare.market: US broadband subscribers of the largest providers (Leichtman Research Group)

threats: Fiber overbuilds by AT&T, Verizon and others and 5G fixed-wireless from T-Mobile and Verizon steadily taking broadband customers (Comcast lost 144,000 domestic broadband customers in Q3 2026)
Continued cord-cutting: 274,000 video customers lost in Q3 2026 alone
Price competition forcing lower broadband ARPU as Comcast moves to guaranteed-price plans and free mobile lines
Execution and dis-synergy risk from the Versant spin-off (Jan 2026) and the planned NBCUniversal/Sky separation expected around mid-2027
Rising sports rights costs (NBA from 2025) and Peacock's long road to steady profits against Netflix, YouTube and Disney
High debt ($87.4 billion at Sep 30, 2026) and heavy network capex
Charter-Cox scale (closed Aug 2026) and possible Paramount-WBD combination strengthening rivals

ceo.name: Brian L. Roberts (Chairman and co-CEO with Mike Cavanagh)
ceo.background: Wharton (University of Pennsylvania) economics graduate and son of Comcast founder Ralph Roberts; joined Comcast in 1981, became president in 1990 and CEO in 2002; Mike Cavanagh, a former JPMorgan CFO, became co-CEO in January 2026 and will lead NBCUniversal after the planned split, with former CFO Michael Angelakis set to become Comcast CEO.

c1.evidence: Comcast leads mature, slow-growing industries (US cable broadband, pay TV, broadcast TV); 2025 revenue of $123,707M was flat versus 2024 and analysts expect declines in 2026-27.

c2.evidence: Customers choose Comcast mainly because its cable network is often the fastest wired option available and bundles with Xfinity Mobile save money, but fiber and fixed-wireless rivals are copying and beating that advantage, as steady broadband losses show.

c3.evidence: Xfinity, NBC, Universal and Peacock are household names and Comcast is a default internet provider in much of the US, but customers rarely recommend it; its satisfaction scores have historically trailed fiber rivals.

c4.evidence: Comcast does not publish a single prominent mission statement; management talks about connectivity, content and shareholder returns, and its recent moves (Versant spin-off, planned NBCUniversal split) are driven by financial value rather than a purpose crusade.

c6.evidence: “big, expensive, bad customer service”; the public knows Xfinity as a powerful but disliked cable company, while NBC, Universal parks and Peacock content are viewed more warmly, so the overall impression is mixed to negative.

c7.evidence: Connectivity, media and parks are huge markets, but US broadband and pay TV are saturated and shrinking for cable; only parks, wireless and streaming are growing, and consensus sees revenue falling about 3% in 2026.

c8.evidence: Comcast has room in wireless (9.3 million lines, about 15% penetration of its broadband base at end-2025), business services and theme parks (Epic Universe 2025, a UK Universal park planned), but no large new markets in its name or technology.

m1.evidence: Brian Roberts built Comcast from a regional cable company into a global media group through bold deals (AT&T Broadband, NBCUniversal, Sky), but he is seen as a dealmaker more than a visionary of the future.

m2.evidence: Roberts is the founder's son, has led for decades, holds Class B shares with one-third of the votes and thinks long-term, but he is not the founder and the company is now splitting itself up.

m4.evidence: Comcast invests in employee programs and was ranked a top-10 Fortune Best Company to Work For in 2024, but its customer-service record has long been criticised.

m5.evidence: Comcast's culture is known for operational discipline and dealmaking rather than a stream of new inventions; its main innovations (X1, Flex, NOW) have not reversed customer losses.

m6.evidence: Roberts is known to be engaged with product (he championed the X1 platform), but he is a business graduate, not an engineer.

m7.evidence: There is no specific evidence that Roberts' stewardship is aimed above profit beyond typical corporate philanthropy such as Project UP digital-equity programs.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech by Brian Roberts at Stanford, Harvard or MIT was found.

m8b.evidence: Roberts is a low-profile, private executive rather than a distinctive public personality like Elon Musk.

m9.evidence: Under Roberts revenue grew from $74.5 billion in 2015 to $123.7 billion in 2025 and diluted EPS from $3.24 (pre-2017 split) to $5.39, but the 2018 Sky acquisition led to an $8.6 billion impairment charge in 2022 and the shares have fallen sharply.

m10.evidence: Comcast is not known for frugality; it spends heavily on sports rights, parks and capex (capital expenditures of $11.75 billion in 2025).

c10.evidence: Comcast's networks connect tens of millions of US homes and its content entertains hundreds of millions, but internet access is a commodity and its products are not life-changing on the scale of Google or Netflix.

p2.evidence: Building and running a national broadband network and blockbuster parks is hard and important for connectivity, but rivals with fiber and wireless can and do replicate it.

f1.evidence: Revenue grew in 2021 ($116,385M), 2022 ($121,427M), 2023 ($121,572M) and 2024 ($123,731M) but slipped to $123,707M in 2025, and is expected to fall in 2026 after the Versant spin-off.

f2.evidence: Operating margin was 16.9% in 2020, 17.9% in 2021, 11.6% in 2022, 19.2% in 2023, 18.8% in 2024 and 16.7% in 2025, so it has not risen.

f3.evidence: Equity is positive ($92.5 billion at Sep 30, 2026) and debt of $87.4 billion is about 2.3x 2025 adjusted EBITDA of $37.4 billion, but it far exceeds cash of $7.6 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating cash flow rose from $24,737M in 2020 to $33,643M in 2025 and operating income from $17,493M to $20,672M, but not steadily (2022 operating income was $14,041M) and 9M 2026 operating income fell to $14,616M from $17,184M.

v1.evidence: Xfinity is not clearly the best broadband product; fiber providers such as AT&T Fiber score higher on satisfaction and often offer symmetric speeds at similar prices.

v2.evidence: Comcast NBCUniversal ranked No. 10 on Fortune's 2024 100 Best Companies to Work For list, but it is not usually counted among the very top employer brands in tech or media.

c5.evidence: If Comcast vanished, tens of millions of homes would lose internet and TV service until rivals filled the gap, and fans would miss NBC sports, Universal films and parks, but most of its services have substitutes.
